\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, by a fixed fraction}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact. From $k\!=\!6$ the panel splits.
Pooled over the panel at $k\ge6$, repeated items are rendered with a median error
of \ErrRep{}\% $[\ErrRepLo{}, \ErrRepHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrRepN{}$), and the error is
one-directional: models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested, never
systematically more. The deficit is roughly constant in relative terms rather
than growing --- \ErrWorstModel{} sits at \ErrWorstVal{}\% across the whole upper
ladder --- so a model asked for $32$ repetitions does not stop at $6$; it stops
at about $27$.

The split matters. \ErrBestModel{}, the largest checkpoint in the panel, shows a
median error of \ErrBestVal{}\% at $k\ge6$: it counts to $32$ without deficit.
The theorem is silent about such a model --- if its per-repetition map does not
contract, no horizon follows --- and we report it as a distinct regime rather
than as a failed prediction. The effect is present in the other
\ErrNSep{} of \ErrNModels{} panel checkpoints with intervals disjoint from their
own controls.

The repeated unit can be a word, a sentence, or a place-value pattern alike.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control item has the
same carrier sentence and the same word count as its repeated twin, and differs
only in that the $k$ copies of one word are replaced by $k$ distinct words. If
the failure were about sequence length, attention span, or accumulated exposure
bias, the two curves would coincide. They do not, and the control result is
categorical: at $k\ge6$ the median control error is \ErrCtl{}\%
$[\ErrCtlLo{}, \ErrCtlHi{}]$ over $n=\ErrCtlN{}$ generations --- \emph{exactly}
the requested number of distinct words, at every $k$ up to $32$, for every model
in the panel. The same decoders that drop one word in six from a repeated
sequence render thirty-two \emph{different} words without a single miscount.

Two further alternatives fail on their own predictions, and the supplement gives
both in full. If repeated text simply being improbable were the cause, the
controls would have to be the more natural member of each pair; scored under a
causal LM outside the panel, the control is the \emph{less} probable member in
\NllIndCtlHigherPct{}\% of the \NllIndPairs{} matched pairs, so naturalness runs
opposite to the effect. If the attractor were acoustic, the horizon would be
counted in tokens, and sentence repetition --- whose unit costs several times more
tokens --- would fail after far fewer repetitions; it does not, differing by
\UnitKDiff{} repetitions while the token count at collapse differs by
\UnitTokRatio{}$\times$.

\subsection{The states the decoder visits stop multiplying}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says the states a decoder visits under periodic
conditioning stop being mutually distinguishable, so asking for more repetitions
should stop buying it distinct internal states while the same amount of
non-repetitive text keeps buying them. We count distinguishable states by the
effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ of the
generation trajectory over normalised singular values; the statistic is the
\emph{capacity gain} $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$,
with intervals bootstrapped over stimulus templates.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain, with disjoint 95\% intervals for
\CapSepPhrase{} panel checkpoints; the matched-pair form of
the comparison gives a positive gap in \CapFracPos{}\% of pairs.

An obvious objection is that this is circular: correctly rendering \emph{very}
sixteen times really does produce monotonous audio, so a low-rank trajectory
might follow from the stimulus rather than from lost capacity. It does not.
Adding realised output diversity (type/token ratio over emitted acoustic tokens,
adjacent-repeat rate, length) as covariates leaves the ratio at \CapAdjRatio{};
restricting to items each model rendered \emph{correctly}, where the audio is by
construction what was asked for, leaves it at \CapCorrRatio{}. The decoder does
not merely err on repeated text --- it runs out of internal states in which an
error and a correct continuation could differ.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} concerns the softmax \emph{restricted to the $k$ repeated
keys}: raw attention weight is normalised over the whole sequence, whose length
grows with $k$, confounding dilution with sequence growth. Renormalised over the
occurrence columns, the profile entropy grows with $\log k$ at slope
\BlockEntropySlope{}, the implied spread is $\delta \le 0.06$ nats across the
ladder, and no occurrence --- not even the most attended --- captures more than
$1.9/k$ of the block's mass: attention over the repeated spans is within a few
percent of uniform, which is what Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} needs. This
covers the \LemBModels{} checkpoints with separable text attention; Qwen3-TTS
sums text and acoustic embeddings per position, so no attention column belongs to
the text and the lemma cannot be checked there.

\subsection{Two things we could not establish}
\label{sec:negative}

We could not measure $q$ itself. Estimating it from boundary distances
($\log\lVert h_{m+1}-h_m\rVert = a + m\log q$) needs a monotone text read-head,
and these decoders' deep-layer attention centroid advances on barely half of
generation steps, so the distances measure localisation error instead. The
failure is self-defeating: the flatter the attention over repeated spans ---
exactly what Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} predicts --- the worse any attention-based
localiser gets. The capacity measure needs no boundaries.

Nor can we claim the count is \emph{absent}: contrasting a ridge probe on the
first and last third of the \emph{same} trajectory, so probe capacity cancels, it
is retained at \ProbeRetRep{} of its early level on repeated text against
\ProbeRetCtl{} on controls --- lower for repeated text in \ProbePhrase{}
checkpoints, but degradation rather than erasure.
